title: Exam Technique and Revision Planning
summary: Build a revision timetable backwards from your exam date, practise recall and past questions properly, manage time per mark and keep calm on exam day.

lessons.title: Working backwards from the exam date

body.p: Revision often fails because students start with the first topic in the book and run out of time before the last. A better way is to start from the exam date and work backwards. You decide how many hours you have, how to split them between subjects, and what you will keep in reserve for practice papers and mistakes.

steps: Write the exam date for each subject and count the weeks you have left.
Be honest about hours you can study each week, after school or lectures, chores, travel, rest and family time.
Multiply weeks by hours to get your total.
Hold back a share of the total for full practice papers and for fixing mistakes.
Split what remains between subjects by weight: more shares for weaker subjects and earlier exams.
Turn each subject's hours into weekly sessions with a clear task.

body.p: Ife has 8 weeks and can study 10 hours a week. That gives 8 x 10 = 80 hours. She holds back 20 percent, which is 16 hours, for timed practice papers and reviewing mistakes. That leaves 64 hours for learning and recall. She has four subjects and rates them by need: Mathematics 3 shares, Chemistry 2, Biology 2 and English 1. That is 8 shares in total, so one share is 64 / 8 = 8 hours.

body.code:
Mathematics  3 shares x 8 = 24 hours  (3 per week)
Chemistry    2 shares x 8 = 16 hours  (2 per week)
Biology      2 shares x 8 = 16 hours  (2 per week)
English      1 share  x 8 = 8 hours   (1 per week)
Practice and mistakes: 16 hours  (2 per week)
Total: 64 + 16 = 80 hours

body.p: Notice that the weekly hours add up to 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 10, matching her available time. If her exam date moves earlier by one week, she can recompute in a minute: 7 weeks gives 70 hours, so she should reduce each share rather than panic.

Your numbers will differ, because every learner has different subjects and different amounts of free time. Weak subjects deserve more shares, but do not drop your strong subjects completely, because they need maintenance too. Always check your own exam dates and the topics you must cover with your teacher or the official syllabus from your exam board.

body.tip: Leave one half day a week empty. Real life will interrupt your plan, and a free slot lets you catch up without wrecking the timetable.

body.p: Reading notes again and again feels productive because the words look familiar. But familiarity is not the same as being able to produce the answer in an exam, when your notes are closed. Active recall means trying to bring information out of your memory before checking it. It is harder, and that effort is what makes it useful.

list: Close the book and write everything you remember about a topic, then check what you missed.
Make question cards with the question on one side and the answer on the other. Paper cards work fine.
Explain a topic aloud to a friend, a sibling or an imaginary class.
Do questions on a topic before you reread the notes.
Draw diagrams, such as a food web or a circuit, from memory and label them.

body.p: Reviewing the same material several times, with gaps between, usually helps you remember it better than one long cram. A simple pattern many learners use is to review after 1 day, 3 days, 7 days and 14 days. These gaps are a guide, not a rule; adjust them to your timetable.

Worked example: Ife learns the topic 'rates of reaction' on Mon 02 Mar. She plans short reviews on Tue 03 Mar, Thu 05 Mar, Mon 09 Mar and Mon 16 Mar. Each review is only 10 minutes. On each, she first writes what she remembers from a blank page, then checks her notes and marks the gaps in a different colour. If she forgets something twice, she adds it to a card pile for extra practice.

steps: After a lesson, write three questions that the lesson could answer.
The next day, answer them without notes.
Check, correct and note the date.
Review again at the next gap, keeping the cards you got wrong in a separate pile.
Retire cards you answer correctly several times in a row, so your pile does not grow forever.

body.p: If this feels uncomfortable, that is normal. Getting things wrong in practice is useful, because it shows you what to fix while there is still time.

body.tip: Put the review dates in your timetable when you first learn a topic. A review that is planned happens; a review you hope to remember often does not.

lessons.title: Practising past questions properly, and learning from mistakes

body.p: Past or practice questions are one of the best tools you have, but only if you use them properly. Many students do a paper, glance at the score and move on. The real value comes from the review: finding out why you lost marks. You should always check which papers are suitable for your own syllabus and exam board, and use the official mark scheme or your teacher's guidance when marking.

Do not start with full papers before you have covered the topics. Early on, do short sets of questions on one topic. Later, move to mixed questions, because the real exam will not tell you which topic comes next.

body.h: Stage 2: sit it under exam conditions

list: Set a timer for the real length of the paper.
Put your phone and notes away.
Write your answers in full, as you would in the exam.
If you must stop a question, mark it and move on, as you would on the day.

body.p: Mark with the official mark scheme if you have it. Give yourself marks only for what you actually wrote, not for what you meant. Then sort every lost mark into a cause, so you can see the pattern.

body.code:
Cause of lost mark        Count   Fix
Did not know the content     6    Re-learn topic, add recall cards
Knew it, misread question    4    Underline command word and numbers
Maths or method slip         3    Show working, check units
Ran out of time              2    Practise time per mark
Vague answer                 3    Use key terms and a reason

body.p: In this example, 18 marks were lost. Content gaps account for 6, but 9 marks were lost through misreading, slips and timing. Re-reading notes would not have fixed those; technique practice will.

steps: Keep a mistake log with the question, the cause and the correct method.
Redo the questions you got wrong after a few days, without looking at the answer.
Re-sit a similar question a week later.
Before the next mock, read your log, not just your notes.

body.tip: After each mock, choose the one most common cause of lost marks and work on that single thing in the next week. Trying to fix everything at once usually fixes nothing.

lessons.title: Reading the question: command words and structure

body.p: Many marks are lost not because a student does not know the topic, but because they answer a different question from the one asked. The command word, usually the first verb, tells you what kind of answer is needed. Different boards may define these words slightly differently, so check your own board's glossary of command words. The meanings below are common general ones.

list: Describe: say what something looks like or what happens, in order, without explaining why.
Explain: give reasons. Use 'because' or 'this leads to'.
Compare: write about similarities and differences, mentioning both items in each point.
Evaluate: weigh strengths and weaknesses, then reach a judgement supported by evidence.
Calculate: work out a number, showing your method, and give units where needed.

body.p: Take the topic of deforestation. 'Describe' wants: 'Large areas of forest are cleared, often for farming or timber, and the number of trees falls.' 'Explain' wants reasons: 'Trees are cleared for farmland because demand for food rises, which reduces habitat, so animals lose their homes.' 'Evaluate' wants a balanced judgement: 'Clearing land provides income and food, but it harms wildlife and soil in the long term. On balance, ... because ...'. Each answer uses the same topic but a different skill.

For short-answer questions, answer the question first, then support it. For longer ones, plan in the margin for 30 seconds, listing the points you will make. A simple pattern is Point, Evidence or example, Explanation. For comparison questions, use words like 'whereas', 'both' and 'however' so the marker sees you are comparing and not only listing.

steps: Circle the command word.
Underline the topic and any limits, such as 'in one country' or 'two reasons'.
Check the marks. Two marks usually means two clear points.
Plan quickly if the answer is long.
Write the answer, using key terms from your subject.
Reread the question and check that you answered it.

body.tip: If a question says 'Give two reasons', writing four does not earn extra credit and wastes time. Write exactly what is asked, and write it well.

body.p: Running out of time is one of the most common reasons strong students underperform. The fix is simple arithmetic done before the exam. Marks tell you how much the examiner expects you to write, and also how much time to spend.

steps: Find the total minutes and total marks of the paper.
Subtract time for checking at the end, for example 10 minutes.
Divide the remaining minutes by the total marks. That gives minutes per mark.
Multiply by the marks on a question to get its time budget.

body.p: A paper has 60 marks and lasts 90 minutes. Keeping 10 minutes for checking leaves 80 minutes. 80 / 60 = 1.33 minutes per mark, which is about 1 minute 20 seconds. So:

body.code:
2-mark question  -> 2.67 min (about 2 min 40 s)
3-mark question  -> 4.0 min
6-mark question  -> 8.0 min
12-mark question -> 16.0 min
Checking time    -> 10 min

body.p: Write these budgets on the top of your paper, or note the clock time you should reach by the end of each section. If you reach the time limit on a question and you are not finished, write a brief ending and move on. Marks are earned fastest at the start of a question, and leaving later questions blank loses easy marks.

Another example: a different paper has 50 marks in 75 minutes with 5 minutes for checking. That gives 70 / 50 = 1.4 minutes per mark, so a 5-mark question gets 7 minutes. Always check the actual length and marks of your own papers, because they differ between subjects and boards.

list: Spend the first minute reading the whole paper and noting which questions are choices.
Start with a question you are confident about to get going, unless your paper must be answered in order.
If you are stuck, mark the question and return later.
Use the checking time to reread the questions and verify calculations, units and missing parts.

body.tip: Practise timing in your mocks. Knowing that you take 9 minutes on a 6-mark question when you have 8 is information you can act on before the real exam.

body.p: Multiple-choice questions look easy because the answer is on the page, but the wrong options are written to attract common mistakes. A calm routine helps you avoid being tricked.

steps: Read the question stem before looking at the options.
Try to answer in your head first.
Read all the options, not just the first one that seems right.
Cross out options that are clearly wrong.
Look for words such as NOT, EXCEPT, always, never and only.
Choose the best remaining option, mark it and move on.

body.p: Suppose a question asks which change would speed up a reaction, and the options include 'lowering the temperature', 'using larger lumps of solid', 'increasing the concentration' and 'removing the catalyst'. If you know that the first, second and fourth would tend to slow the reaction, you are left with the third. You did not need to be certain at the start; you only needed to remove the options you could prove wrong.

A paper has 40 questions in 60 minutes. With 5 minutes kept for checking, you have 55 minutes, or 55 x 60 / 40 = 82.5 seconds per question. If a question takes you more than about a minute and a half, mark it and come back. Whether guessing is wise depends on whether wrong answers lose marks, so check the instructions on your own paper. If there is no penalty, never leave a blank.

list: Do not change an answer without a clear reason, such as spotting a misread word.
Beware of options that are true statements but do not answer the question asked.
For calculations, work out the answer first, then look for it. Check that units match.
On a separate answer sheet, check regularly that your answer is on the matching question number.

body.tip: After a practice test, review every question you got right by guessing as well as those you got wrong. A lucky guess hides a gap in knowledge.

body.p: Good preparation can be wasted by a poor exam day. Most problems are practical and can be prevented: arriving late, forgetting equipment, going without food or water, or sleeping badly after a night of last-minute cramming. This lesson gives practical habits; it is not medical advice, and if you feel overwhelmed for long periods, speak to a teacher, counsellor, parent or someone you trust.

list: Check the time, place and rules for each exam on your official timetable.
Pack your bag: pens, pencils, ruler, calculator if allowed, ID or candidate card, and a clear water bottle if permitted.
Do a light review of your summary sheets and mistake log, not new topics.
Plan how you will travel and leave extra time.
Go to bed at a normal time.

steps: Eat something and drink water, if you can.
Arrive early enough to be settled.
When you get the paper, read all instructions first.
Spend a minute planning your time using minutes per mark.
If your mind goes blank, put your pen down, breathe slowly for a few breaths, and begin with a question you can answer.
Use all the time. Check your answers instead of leaving early.

body.p: Some nervousness is normal and can make you alert. Slow breathing, a short walk before the exam, and a few reminders of what you have already done can help you steady yourself. Avoid comparing notes with others outside the hall before the next paper, since it often creates worry and cannot change what you wrote. Instead, take a short break, eat, and focus on the next exam.

Amara realises halfway through a 12-mark question that she has misread it. She has used 10 of her 16 minutes. She crosses out a short section, writes 'see below', and starts again, aiming at the correct command word with a quick three-point plan. She does not finish perfectly, but she scores marks on the right points and keeps time for later questions. Staying calm and acting quickly beat panicking.

When an exam is over, do not replay it for hours. Note one thing you would do differently, then move on to the next paper. Once all exams are done, reviewing what worked will help you with future exams.

body.tip: Make a one-page exam-day checklist now and read it the night before. A tired brain forgets simple things.

quiz.q: You have 6 weeks, 10 study hours a week and 3 subjects. You decide to hold back 20 percent for practice papers and mistakes. How many hours remain for learning and recall?
options: 60 hours
12 hours
48 hours
54 hours

quiz.q: Your timetable is built for 8 weeks, but the exam is moved one week earlier. What is the best response?
options: Ignore the change and keep the old 8-week timetable, hoping you can simply study faster each day
Recompute the hours for 7 weeks, trim each subject's share and keep the practice and mistake time
Drop all the practice papers and mistake review so that every topic still fits into the shorter time
Study through the nights in the final week to make up the lost week of study time

quiz.q: It is the day after you learned a topic. Which activity is the best use of 10 minutes?
options: Write down all you can remember from a blank page, then check your notes
Reread the notes twice, so that the topic feels familiar to you again
Copy your notes out neatly in a new colour so they look organised
Highlight the main points again in a bright colour, then read them over

quiz.q: Why is it useful to review a topic after 1, 3, 7 and 14 days instead of once for a long session?
options: Short sessions are better than long ones for every topic, whatever its type
Spaced reviews give repeated chances to retrieve it just as it starts to fade
It means you can stop learning new material once the schedule starts
Exam boards require the exact gaps of 1, 3, 7 and 14 days for every student

quiz.q: After a mock, you lost 18 marks: 6 from not knowing content, 4 from misreading, 3 from slips, 2 from time and 3 from vague answers. What does the pattern suggest?
options: Content is the only real problem because it cost the most marks of any one cause, so reread all your notes
Most lost marks came from technique, so practise reading, showing working and timing as well as content
The mock paper was probably unfair, so ignore the result and simply move on to a new set of papers this week
Nothing useful can be learned from a mock in which so many marks were lost, so skip analysis

quiz.q: You score 62 percent on a past paper. What is the most valuable next step?
options: Mark each lost mark by cause, record it in a mistake log, and redo those questions days later
Move on to a new paper straight away, to cover more ground before the exam arrives and time runs short
Read the mark scheme once, feel reassured about the score, and put the paper away
Repeat the same paper the next day and memorise the model answers word for word until they feel automatic

quiz.q: A question says: 'Explain why the number of trees falls when land is cleared for farming.' Which answer best fits the command word?
options: The number of trees falls when land is cleared, which is exactly what the question already says
Farming is good because it produces food and income for families and the country
Trees are cut down because farmland is needed, so fewer remain and habitats are lost
There are many different types of trees in many countries across the world and continents

quiz.q: A question asks you to 'Evaluate' two ways of generating electricity. What should your answer include?
options: A detailed list of facts about only one of the methods, with no comparison
A clear description of how each method works, but with no judgement at the end
Strengths and weaknesses of each, then a judgement supported by reasons
One sentence saying which method you personally prefer, with no reasons

quiz.q: A paper has 60 marks and lasts 90 minutes. You keep 10 minutes for checking. About how long should a 6-mark question take?
options: 9 minutes
6 minutes
12 minutes
8 minutes

quiz.q: A paper has 50 marks in 75 minutes, with 5 minutes for checking. A 5-mark question has already taken you 10 minutes and you are not finished. What should you do?
options: Keep going until the answer is perfect, even if that leaves later questions blank
Cross out the answer, leave the question blank and refuse to return to it later
Spend another 10 minutes on it, since the marks here count the same as any other
Write a short conclusion, move on and return if time remains, as the budget was 7 minutes

quiz.q: In a multiple-choice question where wrong answers lose no marks, you know two options are clearly wrong but are unsure about the other two. What is the best next step?
options: Pick the first of the remaining two options without reading the question again
Leave it blank to be safe, even though there is no penalty for wrong answers
Spend five more minutes on it before looking at any other questions on the paper
Reread for key words, pick the better of the two remaining options and move on

quiz.q: In a 40-question multiple-choice paper lasting 60 minutes with 5 minutes for checking, about how long can you give each question?
options: About 90 seconds
About 60 seconds
About 2 minutes
About 82 seconds

quiz.q: The night before an exam, you feel you have not covered a whole topic. What is the most sensible plan?
options: Spend a set time on a summary of the topic, then rest, check your bag and sleep normally
Stay up all night learning everything you missed so that nothing is left uncovered in the exam
Skip the review and watch videos until late to relax your mind before the exam starts tomorrow
Give up on the exam, since one uncovered topic means you are bound to fail it

quiz.q: Halfway through the exam your mind goes blank on a question. What should you do?
options: Pause, breathe slowly, then move to a question you can answer and return later
Stare at the question for as long as it takes until the answer comes back to you
Leave the exam hall at once, since your mind blanking means you cannot continue
Start writing anything that comes to mind on every question, to fill the pages

quiz.q: Outside the exam hall, friends compare answers to the paper you just finished, and you start to worry. What is a helpful response?
options: Join in and check each of your answers against theirs to see how you did
Step away, have a drink and a snack, and focus on the next paper
Decide you have failed and stop revising for the other papers this week
Rewrite your answers on a piece of paper to see if you were right
